strengths: Addresses a clearly stated open problem: the first Best-of-Both-Worlds (BoBW) guarantees for episodic MDPs with heavy-tailed feedback, in both known-transition and unknown-transition settings, which existing HTMDP literature (Zhuang & Sui 2021, etc.) does not cover.

The technical toolkit is substantive and not a trivial transplant from bandits: the skipping loss estimator adapted to occupancy measures, the local control of heavy-tailed shifted losses (Lemmas B.2/B.3 with a decomposition into centered loss and differential value terms), and the suboptimal-mass propagation lemma (Lemma B.8/B.4) are genuinely new ingredients needed to make FTRL-with-Tsallis BoBW analysis work under unbounded feedback.

The main results are meaningful: nearly minimax-optimal Oe(T^{1/α}) adversarial regret with O(log T) stochastic regret for known transitions, and Oe(T^{1/α} + √T) with O(log² T) for unknown transitions; the bounds recover Jin & Luo (2020)/Jin et al. (2021) at α=2 and match heavy-tailed MAB lower bounds in the bandit reduction, supporting tightness.

The regret decomposition for the unknown-transition case (TransErr/EstReg/SkipErr/PessErr) and the pessimistic estimator with upper occupancy bounds is a sensible and clearly explained design, and the appendices provide fairly detailed end-to-end proofs including explicit constants (Eqs. 16-17).
The related-work coverage is thorough (main text plus a substantial appendix), and the paper is honest about what is inherited from prior work versus new.
weaknesses: Inconsistencies between theorem statements in the main text and the formal appendix versions reduce confidence: e.g., Theorem 5.1 states an adversarial bound with a √(T log T) and log(T)² term, while Theorem C.1 states Oe(H^{α+1}S^{2−1/α}A^{5−4/α}σT^{1/α} + HσS√(AT)); the poly(H,S,A) factors are also stated differently in Theorem 4.1 versus Theorem B.1. These should be reconciled.

Several proof steps in Appendix C are abbreviated to the point of being unverifiable: Lemma C.8 says 'Similar analysis in Lemma 4.2 shows that…', Lemma C.9's key inequality (splitting SkipErr and bounding the UOB-deviation term) drops cross-terms and sign handling with limited justification, and parts of B.10/B.5 rely on 'negative terms vanished' arguments that deserve formal treatment. Given these are the novel parts, the soundness of the full unknown-transition result is harder to fully verify.

The algorithm requires prior knowledge of the tail parameters (α, σ) to set C, β, and D; for heavy-tailed MABs, parameter-free BoBW algorithms exist (Chen et al. 2025), so this is a notable practical and conceptual limitation that is only mentioned as future work rather than discussed as a limitation.

No lower bounds are given for the HTMDP self-bounding/stochastic regime; the log T (and log² T) guarantees are argued to be tight only via reduction to the MAB lower bound, so the optimality of the instance-dependent rates in the MDP setting remains open.

There is no empirical evaluation or even a discussion of computational aspects beyond noting that the FTRL subproblem is a convex program solvable in polynomial time (the Comp-UOB procedure's cost is likewise not quantified); for an ICML audience, even a small-scale experiment illustrating the skipping estimator's behavior would strengthen the contribution.

Presentation quality is uneven: heavy reliance on 'poly(H,S,A)' hides dependence that is later shown to be quite large (e.g., A^{5−5α}), and some notation (ut vs. ρ vs. xt in the unknown-transition estimator) is used loosely in the text describing Algorithm 2, making the estimator construction harder to parse than necessary.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly-motivated open problem: existing HTMDP literature (Zhuang & Sui 2021 and follow-ups) is limited to stochastic regimes with polynomial regret, and existing BoBW-MDP results (Jin & Luo 2020; Jin et al. 2021) crucially require bounded/sub-Gaussian losses. This paper gives the first Best-of-Both-Worlds guarantees for heavy-tailed MDPs, in both known- and unknown-transition settings.

The headline results are strong in their T-dependence: O(T^{1/α}) instance-independent adversarial regret for known transitions and O(T^{1/α}+√T) for unknown transitions, matching the lower bounds of Bubeck et al. (2013) and Zhuang & Sui (2021) in T, σ up to logarithmic factors; simultaneously achieving O(log T) (known transition) and O(log²T) (unknown transition) instance-dependent regret in self-bounding regimes. The α=2 case recovers Jin et al. (2021) up to poly(H,S,A) factors.
The self-bounding formulation (Definition 3.1) covers not only stochastic environments but also corrupted-stochastic settings, making the stochastic result more broadly useful.

The analysis contains real technical work beyond plugging existing tools together: the local decomposition of the heavy-tailed shifted skipping loss into centered loss and differential value function terms (Lemmas 4.2/4.3, B.2/B.3), the suboptimal-mass propagation lemma (Lemma 4.4/B.8) which handles the difficulty that the reference occupancy measure is spread over states (unlike MABs), and the four-term regret decomposition (TransErr/EstReg/SkipErr/PessErr) for the unknown-transition case with a pessimistic UOB-weighted estimator. The proofs in Appendices B and C are carried out at a detailed level, including constant choices (Eqs. 16–17).

The main text is generally well-organized: challenges are articulated clearly, the roadmap of the analysis (stability, penalty, skipping terms) helps readability, and related work is thorough (including an extensive appendix-level discussion).
weaknesses: Novelty is largely combinatorial/adaptational. The skeleton (FTRL over occupancy measures with Tsallis regularizer, loss shifting, doubling epochs, UOB) is taken from Jin et al. (2020/2021), and the skipping/truncation idea with skipping bonus is from heavy-tailed MABs (Huang et al. 2022; Zhao et al. 2025). The paper's claim of technical innovation is defensible, but the contribution is an extension of known machinery to a new setting rather than a new algorithmic principle.

The dependence on H, S, A is very large and likely loose (e.g., adversarial unknown-transition bound scales like H^{α+1}S^{2-1/α}A^{5-4/α}; self-bounding terms like H^4σ²S³A²log²(ι)). No lower bounds are given for these factors, so the near-optimality claim applies only to the T, σ, and gap dependence. This significantly limits the practical relevance of the bounds.

The algorithm requires prior knowledge of the tail parameters (α, σ) and problem dimensions (through constants C, β, D), whereas recent heavy-tailed bandit work (e.g., Chen et al. 2025, uniINF) has moved to parameter-free designs. This gap is acknowledged only implicitly via future work.

There are inconsistencies and sloppiness in the appendix that undermine confidence: e.g., Lemma C.7 claims |ℓ̂_t(s,a)| ≤ O(t²) while the displayed derivation with u_t ≥ 1/(St) and τ_t = O(t^{1/α}) suggests a larger order (the term is only used on a T^{-3}-probability event, but the statement as written appears incorrect); the exponent '1/α+1' in Eq. (50) does not match the τ_t scaling; Lemma C.9 is stated 'under E' in Appendix C.5 but 'with high probability' in the main text; the formal adversarial bound in Theorem C.1 differs in form from Theorem 5.1 (missing the log²(T) and √(T log T) terms). These should be fixed and verified.

Some steps in the proofs are compressed with appeals to 'similar analysis in Lemma X' (e.g., Eq. (52) relying on Lemma B.6 under the empirical model, and the transition-error bounds deferred wholesale to Jin et al. 2021 Eqs. (36-38)); verifying that these transfers are valid under the modified estimator (UOB-weighted importance sampling rather than exact occupancy) requires effort that the paper does not fully document.

No empirical evaluation whatsoever. For an algorithms paper this is not disqualifying, but even a small numerical illustration of the skipping estimator's behavior (e.g., sensitivity to the skipping constant C, empirical regret in mixed stochastic/adversarial environments) would substantiate the practical claims made in the introduction about heavy-tailed real-world feedback.

Significance is somewhat specialized: the result is a clean closure of a specific open question at the intersection of two literatures (BoBW-MDPs and heavy-tailed bandits), but the heavy poly factors and parameter knowledge requirements mean the practical impact is limited, and follow-up work will likely be needed to tighten these aspects.

strengths: The paper resolves a clearly stated open problem: it gives the first Best-of-Both-Worlds guarantees for episodic MDPs with heavy-tailed feedback, in both the known-transition and unknown-transition settings. The results (Õ(T^{1/α}) adversarial / O(log T) stochastic for known transitions; Õ(T^{1/α}+√T) adversarial / O(log²T) stochastic for unknown transitions) match the known lower bounds in T up to logarithmic factors, and recover Jin & Luo (2020)/Jin et al. (2021) when α=2.

The technical machinery is genuinely novel rather than a black-box combination: the occupancy-adaptive skipping loss estimator (Algorithm 1, Eqs. 2-3), the local control of heavy-tailed shifted losses (Lemmas 4.2/4.3, proved via a centered-loss/differential-value decomposition with a careful reachability-weight argument), the suboptimal mass propagation lemma (Lemma 4.4), and the four-term regret decomposition (TransErr/EstReg/SkipErr/PessErr) with a pessimistic estimator over Upper Occupancy Bounds are all new contributions that could be of independent interest.

The setting is more general than much prior heavy-tailed work: losses may be unbounded and negative, with only a bounded α-moment assumed, and no non-negativity assumption is needed (unlike Huang et al. 2022).

The appendices contain a substantial, mostly careful proof effort (Bregman-divergence FTRL analysis with Tsallis entropy stability from Ito et al. 2024, epoch-based analysis with high-probability confidence sets, Young's inequality balancing for self-bounding bounds), and the related-work section is thorough and accurately positions the contribution.
weaknesses: At least one step in the unknown-transition analysis appears unjustified as written. In the proof of Lemma C.9, the bound E[ℓskip]·(u_t − ρ^{P,πt})/u_t·(x_t − ρ̂^{π̂}) ≤ 2σ·Σ|u_t − ρ^{P,πt}| implicitly requires |x_t(s,a) − ρ̂^{P̂,π̂}(s,a)| = O(u_t(s,a)). However, u_t(s,a) upper-bounds the occupancy of the exploration policy πt over the confidence set, not that of the benchmark π̂; when πt rarely visits (s,a) but π̂ does, ρ̂^{π̂}(s,a) can be close to 1 while u_t(s,a) is small, so the inequality does not obviously hold (it is rescued at x_t=0 only because τ_t=0 forces ℓskip=0, but not for small positive x_t with large ρ̂^{π̂}). This step affects the UOB-deviation term underlying the √T adversarial bound and needs a rigorous justification or repair.

Several other proof steps are compressed in ways that impede verification: Lemma C.8's 'naive bound' glosses over constants ('ignoring the constant terms'), Lemma C.7 uses a crude O(t²) fallback whose propagation through the epoch sums is not spelled out, and there are minor inconsistencies between main-text and appendix statements (e.g., Lemma 4.2 vs. Lemma B.2 constants; H vs. H² in Lemma B.6; occasional exponent drift such as A^{5-4/α} vs. A^{5-5/α}). These do not appear fatal but lower confidence in full correctness without independent checking.

The algorithms require prior knowledge of the tail parameters (α, σ), and the skipping constant C depends on H, S, A. Recent heavy-tailed bandit work the paper itself cites (Chen et al. 2025, uniINF) achieves parameter-free BoBW; the lack of any adaptivity discussion or even a limitations paragraph on this point is a notable gap.

The polynomial dependence on H, S, A is very loose (e.g., A^{5-4/α} in the unknown-transition adversarial bound, H^4σ^2S^3A^2 log²(ι) in the stochastic bound). The authors acknowledge this as future work, but it means the 'near minimax-optimality' claim holds only in T, and the α=2 recovery of Jin et al. (2021) is up to polynomial factors in H, S, A. Also, optimality for the known-transition case is argued by reduction to MAB lower bounds rather than an HTMDP-specific lower bound.

There is no empirical evaluation whatsoever, and the per-episode computational cost of solving the convex program over Q(P) (or Comp-UOB) is not analyzed beyond a claim of polynomial time; even synthetic experiments on heavy-tailed MDPs or a runtime discussion would have strengthened the paper.

The self-bounding bound for unknown transitions requires the balancing condition α'+β'+γ' ≤ 1/2, which the proof says holds 'when Csb is not too small'; the case analysis technically covers this via Case 1, but the presentation here is sloppy and the interplay between the two cases is not cleanly stated.
